content: Adult patients who test positive for HBsAg should be treated with antiviral therapy as a standard practice, regardless of their HBV DNA levels, HBeAg status, or ALT levels. The World Health Organization (WHO) is currently revising its guidelines for the prevention, care, and treatment of individuals with chronic hepatitis B infection. As part of this process, the WHO conducted a survey to assess the values and preferences of healthcare workers regarding the treatment of children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis B. This survey was conducted online in March and April 2023. The survey aimed to address two primary questions: which children should be prioritized for treatment, and which antiviral regimens should be used. It was distributed to nine networks of healthcare providers caring for children and adolescents with hepatitis B, with respondents encouraged to share the survey within their networks. A total of 150 healthcare workers from 41 countries across all six WHO regions participated in the survey. Most respondents were pediatricians (70%) working in tertiary care centers (80%). The most commonly used drugs for treating children and adolescents with hepatitis B over the past five years were tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), entecavir, and lamivudine. These drugs were also the most frequently registered and licensed in the respondents' countries and were often provided through national insurance or government-funded programs. When deciding whom to treat, healthcare workers prioritized adolescents and children with elevated ALT levels or those who were immunosuppressed. Other factors influencing treatment decisions included HBeAg status, ALT levels, viral load, and evidence of liver fibrosis. Only a small number of respondents indicated they would treat all children and adolescents with hepatitis B. Half of the respondents believed that treatment criteria for adolescents should be the same as for adults. However, 69% suggested that treatment criteria for children aged 0–11 years should differ from those for adults. The main reasons cited for this differentiation included the immune-tolerant phase and normal ALT levels in children, the absence of fibrosis and cirrhosis, and the lower likelihood of developing hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Concerns about treatment adherence, the need to establish appropriate dosing for children, and potential toxicity and side effects, particularly on growth, were also highlighted. Regarding drug regimens, most respondents (69%) agreed that the choice of antiviral therapy for adolescents should align with that for adults. However, only 17% believed that treatments for children should be the same as for adults. Safety concerns, the impact on growth and development, and the need for child-specific formulations were the primary reasons for preferring different regimens for children. The survey findings provide valuable insights into the priorities and preferences of healthcare workers worldwide regarding the treatment of children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis B. These findings will inform the development of updated WHO guidelines, which aim to expand treatment eligibility criteria, simplify diagnostic and treatment pathways, and improve access to care for individuals with hepatitis B.
